item.mechanism: High pressure induces a polymorphic transition from fcc to hcp by overcoming kinetic barriers, facilitated by the alloy's low stacking fault energy which allows local stacking fault introduction.
item.operating_conditions: Room temperature, hydrostatic compression up to ~41 GPa using helium as pressure-transmitting medium
item.supporting_observation: Phase transition starts at ~22 GPa, completes at ~41 GPa, and the hcp phase is retained upon decompression to ambient pressure.
item.scope_limits: The transition is described as sluggish and irreversible; the authors note that at ambient pressure and room temperature, the fcc phase is kinetically stable and the transition is hindered.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors mention that stacking faults, dislocations, and twinning events may be involved, and that magnetic states could affect the behavior.
quotes: recent experiment [41] and simulations [37] [41] have confirmed that it indeed has a low staking fault energy of ∼20 mJ m −2
high-pressure can help overcome the kinetic barrier between hcp and fcc HEAs

item.mechanism: Temperature drives the reverse transition from hcp to fcc because the fcc phase is entropically stabilized and thermodynamically favorable at high temperatures.
item.operating_conditions: Temperatures up to ~1,400 K at pressures of 6, 14, and 26 GPa; up to 723 K at ambient pressure
item.supporting_observation: The hcp phase transforms back to fcc when heated above ~633 K at ambient pressure and above ~1,400 K at 26 GPa.
item.scope_limits: The authors state that the observed transition temperatures represent a synthesis curve (first appearance of fcc) rather than the true equilibrium boundary due to kinetic barriers.
item.alternatives_considered: The text notes that the real equilibrium phase boundary may be much lower than observed due to overshooting caused by high energy barriers.
quotes: the fcc phase is stable at high temperatures while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at relatively lower temperatures
the temperature of ∼1,400 K was determined to be the critical temperature ( fcc -in) for the phase transition
The real equilibrium phase boundary between fcc and hcp may be much lower than 633 K observed in experiments

item.mechanism: The fcc structure is a metastable polymorph formed by kinetic constraints during conventional preparation (melt casting/atomization) because high-temperature polymorphs form first according to Ostwald's Rule.
item.operating_conditions: Conventional preparation techniques such as melt casting and gas atomization
item.supporting_observation: The alloy always forms the fcc structure first upon cooling from the melt, preventing the transition to the thermodynamically favored hcp phase at room temperature.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism applies to conventional synthesis; it does not hold for the hcp phase synthesized via high-pressure compression.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors consider that nano-twinning at cryogenic temperatures might facilitate the fcc-to-hcp transition by diminishing stacking fault energy.
quotes: According to Ostwald's Rule [44] , high-temperature polymorphs often form first during cooling/crystallization
with conventional preparation techniques such as melt casting and atomization, the CoCrFeMnNi HEA always forms the fcc structure first
the transition from fcc to hcp likely depends on the entire complex γ -surface and could be kinetically hindered

item.mechanism: Pressure tunes the volume and energy state of the alloy, making the hcp structure thermodynamically favorable over fcc at lower temperatures and higher pressures.
item.operating_conditions: High pressure (up to 26 GPa) combined with elevated temperature
item.supporting_observation: The critical temperature for the hcp-to-fcc transformation rises as pressure increases, indicating a positive slope in the phase boundary.
item.scope_limits: The mechanism relies on the similarity in volume and bulk modulus between the two phases, which allows for a weak first-order transition.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors note that the transition could be influenced by magnetic states, though the primary driver identified is pressure-induced volume tuning.
quotes: As pressure is increased, the critical temperature for the hcp -to- fcc transformation also rises
Compared with temperature, pressure is a more powerful parameter in terms of decreasing the volume, tuning packing and energy state of a sample
the hcp phase of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA is relatively stable at low temperatures and high pressures

item.mechanism: Coexistence of fcc and hcp phases over a wide pressure range is attributed to very similar free energies of the two phases and/or large energy barriers between them.
item.operating_conditions: Pressure range between ~22 GPa and ~41 GPa
item.supporting_observation: Diffraction patterns show fcc and hcp peaks coexisting over a large pressure range, and decompression yields composites with tunable fractions.
item.scope_limits: The authors do not quantify the exact free energy difference but infer it from the coexistence and sluggishness of the transition.
item.alternatives_considered: The text suggests that the transition is martensitic-like with weak first-order features, similar to cobalt or xenon.
quotes: both the fcc and hcp can coexist over a wide pressure range (∼22 to ∼41 GPa), which could be attributed to the very similar free energy of the fcc and hcp phases and/or the large energy barrier between them
The transition was sluggish, the fcc and new phase coexisted over large pressure range
This is similar to many other fcc to hcp martensitic transitions, such as in cobalt [39] or xenon [40]

item.mechanism: Decreasing temperature reduces stacking fault energy, facilitating the sliding needed for a displacive phase transition from fcc to hcp.
item.supporting_observation: Nano-twinning has been observed at cryogenic temperatures, supporting the speculation that stacking fault energy diminishes with decreasing temperature.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism explains potential transitions at cryogenic temperatures but was not directly observed as a full phase transition in this specific study.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors reference recent theoretical work confirming the temperature dependence of stacking fault energy.
quotes: nano-twinning has been observed in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA at cryogenic temperatures (77 K)
This observation indicates that the stacking fault energy may diminish with decreasing temperature, which could facilitate the sliding needed for a displacive phase transition from fcc to hcp
Recent theoretical work studied the stacking fault energy as a function of temperature in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA and confirmed this speculation

item.mechanism: The fcc and hcp lattices differ only in stacking sequence (ABCABC vs ABAB), allowing hcp to form locally from fcc via stacking faults.
item.operating_conditions: General structural context, applicable during compression
item.supporting_observation: The hcp (002) and (110) planes inherit from fcc (111) and (220) planes, respectively, indicating a structural relationship.
item.scope_limits: The detailed mechanism is noted to be complex, involving dislocations and twinning beyond simple stacking faults.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors acknowledge that the mechanism could be much more complex than simple stacking fault introduction.
quotes: the fcc and hcp lattices only differ in the stacking sequence of the close packing layers
The hcp structure can be readily obtained locally from a fcc structure by introducing stacking faults
it is clear that the hcp -(002) and hcp -(110) planes inherit the fcc -(111) and fcc -(220) planes, respectively

item.mechanism: The polymorphic transition behavior is expected to be general in various high-entropy alloys at certain pressure and temperature conditions due to the fundamental nature of fcc-hcp packing.
item.operating_conditions: Certain pressure and temperature conditions (not specified for all HEAs)
item.supporting_observation: The authors propose that the transition is not limited to CoCrFeMnNi and could provide model systems for understanding fcc-hcp packing in statistical physics.
item.scope_limits: The statement is a generalization based on the CoCrFeMnNi results; specific conditions for other HEAs are not detailed.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors note that the transition is entropy-dominated in hard sphere systems, suggesting a universal thermodynamic driver.
quotes: The polymorphic transition discovered in this work is by no means limited to this specific CoCrFeMnNi HEA
we expect that this behaviour could be general in various HEAs at certain pressure and temperature conditions
the transition between fcc and hcp is believed to be entropy dominated
